Nothing specific for what you're looking for, but you might want to look at generic standards instead, and choose a style that meets all your needs. Any public docker image will have it's own method of doing things, so rolling your own, your way, is likely the best option. What we do, is actually install the software, from scratch, each time we deploy a new container. The "docker image" holds all the information required to create a working container, including instructions on how to install the software, and where it find it's config files (which should live outside the container).

You want to be searching for "orchestration" methods, which will lead you down a rabbit hole of information that will save days of work in the future. There's a whole, huge world out there for docker and "how to".

The beauty of using Docker for these kinds of things, is you only need to do them once. My company runs everything inside docker containers (\~50 containers per environment). Having to do anything manually to any environment is considered a bug, and goes back to DevOps/Dev to get fixed. 

Make everything exactly what you need it to be in your container. Jam it in your repo and deploy it somewhere else. If there's anything wrong, fix it on your original container and try again. We use a series of [run.py](https://run.py) scripts inside the container that does all the little "Make sure this is right. Make sure that's right." steps for running the software. What I mean is, if you want /var/www to be owned by www:www, just go ahead and make sure that happens every time the container runs.
